name: Archetype: steppe nomad confederations

weightNotes.aggression: Constant raiding of settled neighbours, but set battles were avoided unless the odds were good (Scythians against Darius 513 BC refused battle). Mid.
weightNotes.maneuver: Wholly mounted armies with remount herds; mobility was the whole system (Mounted archery; Hildinger, Warriors of the Steppe).
weightNotes.flanking: Envelopment by horse archers and the feigned flight into an ambush were standard (Parthian shot, Scythian and Hunnic practice).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Before the Mongols most confederations could not take walled cities except by surprise, starvation or hired engineers (Huns at Orleans 451 failed to finish the siege). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Bands dispersed to harass and regrouped; some held a lancer reserve, mostly not.
weightNotes.scouting: Steppe life made every rider a scout and wide screens were normal; below the Mongol 0.95 because intelligence networks were less systematic.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Nomad units broke contact early by design and returned later; avoiding attrition was the doctrine. Lowest of all profiles.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Horse archers dominant with some noble heavy lancers; no infantry or siege arm worth the name in most cases.
weightNotes.initiative: Clan and tribal bands acting under their own chiefs within a loose confederation: decentralised, but also poorly coordinated, so mid.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived on herds and plunder and raided far beyond any supply network; campaigns were seasonal and limited by grass. Low strictness.

summary: Pastoral confederations (Scythians, Xiongnu, Huns, Avars, Magyars, Cumans and later Turkic and Mongol successors) fought as mounted archers with several horses per man. They raided settled states, avoided battle on bad terms, harassed with arrows, feigned flight to break the enemy's formation and finished with lancers. When invaded they retreated into the steppe, stripping pasture and blocking wells until the invader starved.
whyItWorked: Settled armies could not catch them or bring them to battle, and their bows out-ranged infantry on open ground. The steppe itself was a defence: no city to capture, and an invader's supply could not follow. Darius I's Scythian campaign (513 BC) ended in withdrawal against scorched earth and refusal of battle.
whereItFailed: When a settled state built its own cavalry and logistics and pushed into the steppe: Mobei (119 BC), where Han armies under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeated the Xiongnu. When forced to fight heavy troops on ground they could not leave or after plunder slowed them: Lechfeld (955) for the Magyars. Against walls and combined Roman-Germanic coalitions: the Catalaunian Plains (451) and Orleans for the Huns. Confederations also broke up on a leader's death.
